newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem return to villages may be military - NATO.
newsitem.headline: Moslem return to villages may be military - NATO.

text.p: The Moslem occupation of three destroyed villages on Serb territory, billed by the Bosnian government as the innocent returns of refugees, could mask a military motive, NATO warned on Monday.

"The villages are a few kilometres from the Drina river. It doesn't take a genius to figure they could be jumping-off points for an army effort one day to cut the Serb republic in half," said a NATO officer who asked not to be named.
"The Moslems have built a new road and a substantial bridge connecting the area to Tuzla. We're seeing a clever military move under the cover of civilian refugee returns."
The Bosnian government says there was no ulterior motive behind a natural desire by refugees to return to their homes.

The three villages, Dugi Dio, Mahala and Jusici, lie in an area of northeastern Bosnia known as the Sapna Thumb, a slice of territory flanked on three sides by Serb forces but fiercely defended by Moslems during 43-months of war.
Serb attacks during the conflict nibbled away at the thumb or tried to cut it off altogether.
The Moslem objective was to reach the Drina river, Bosnia's border with rump Yugoslavia to the east, and thereby split Bosnian Serb territory in two.
When the war ended in December 1995, the Moslems were just 10 km (six miles) from their goal.
The Dayton peace accord turned former front lines into a de facto border between Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and its Serb republic.
Although Dayton guaranteed refugees displaced by the war the right to return to their homes, only a few hundred have risked crossing ethnic boundary lines.
Most of those have been Moslems returning to the Sapna thumb area or to Brcko, a town on the Sava river whose fate is supposed to be decided by arbitration by the end of the year.
The Serb republic is only a few kilometres (miles) wide at Brcko as well.
"I don't think it's an accident the returns have been concentrated in the strategically vital areas of Sapna and Brcko," said the NATO source.

"Large-scale refugee returns are a dead letter, at least for the moment. They just aren't occurring. The Moslems are building a bridgehead in two vital locations. Not for any imminent military action but for some time in the future."
The village of Dugi Dio was on the Moslem side of the "inter-entity boundary line" (IEBL) when the war ended but was then transferred to Serb control. Moslems refused to leave.
Moslems crossed the IEBL to enter neighbouring Mahala and Jusici and reclaim their homes. Some arrived with arms, violating rules in a NATO-enforced "Zone of Separation".
Many of those returning were military age men. In both villages NATO forces were required to intervene to prevent serious violence between Moslems and Serb authorities.
For the past 10 days NATO officers and international mediators have been trying to broker an agreement between the parties to regulate refugee returns on a broader scale.
They want the Moslems occupying Jusici to leave and apply for permission to return, a proposal neither the refugees nor their leaders have so far been willing to accept.
